1 big thing: Surviving chaos
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

Jim VandeHei has warned us that we're locked in a new, sustained period of constant, wild, holy-crap changes — good and bad. AI is the instigator. Here are some pointers on how we can survive and thrive, adapted from this weekend's edition of his Axios CEO newsletter:

Many of you feel your company is moving quicker than ever, sometimes with dizzying changes and too little explanation. My aim is to take you inside the way heads of organizations are thinking, or should be.

  • For leaders, this is a survival guide. And these changes are trickling down to every single employee. So if you're not the boss, I want to help you adapt, contribute and ask better questions.

Forget wartime vs. peacetime CEOs. That choice seems quaint.

Why it matters: Ben Horowitz's famous war vs. peace frame dates to 2011. It assumed companies were in war mode (start-ups or scaling fast) or peace mode (established, maturing) based on circumstance. Truth is, we're all Chaos CEOs or working for Chaos-Era Companies now.

  • Chaos CEO, simplified: Leaders built for the speed of "post-processable velocity" with the smarts to calmly navigate constant, infinite chain reactions.

🔄 A quick refresher:

  • Post-processable velocity = events outrunning our ability to keep up.
  • Infinite chain reactions = politics, AI, media and business blending and immediately bleeding into each other.

Most leadership jobs now require the best of both wartime and peacetime skills, as well as brand-new muscles:

  • Panoramic vision. Tech, politics, media and markets now collide. We can't understand our company by watching our industry. The unexpected hits come from adjacent spaces.
  • Split-screen vision. We need to see both the whole field panoramically and the next call in front of us. We need to be better at thinking big and small at the same time.
  • Quicker twitch. I told the Axios board our confident line of sight is six weeks, tops. So we need to decide in weeks, not quarters. Move fast on anything reversible. Slow down only for what we can't undo.
  • AI fluency. Old-school CEOs could delegate on tech, both in war and peace. We can't. If we aren't using the models, we can't judge what's now possible.
  • Shift-and-say. Wartime CEOs commit and never blink. Chaos CEOs update just as fast — and publicly — with zero ego about shifting and quickly explaining those adjustments. Context matters, both for informing staff and fine-tuning AI agents. Constant overcommunication soars in importance.
  • Solid core. The more everything moves, the more our people need the two or three things that won't: values, standards and our theory of the case. We need to stress these constantly.
  • Wartime urgency, peacetime calm. The wartime CEO of Horowitz's telling is a bulldozer. That fails now. Our people are already rattled. Chaos outside demands calm inside.
  • Chaos is a ladder. Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron is repurposing this "Game of Thrones" lingo. In the chaos, we can find new opportunities to climb toward.

2. 🌊 House Dems clinch historic 258 seats
 
Data: Ballotpedia. Chart: Axios Visuals

With 258 seats and counting, Democrats have clinched the biggest House majority for either party since the early 1990s.

  • Democrats hit that number yesterday after North Carolina Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, chair of the powerful Rules Committee. (Go deeper)
  • Four races remain uncalled: Democrats lead by fewer than 350 votes in Minnesota's 1st District and Tennessee's 4th District. Two Louisiana races are headed to runoffs next month.

🔭 Zoom in: Democrats will hold at least as many seats as they did after Bill Clinton's first win in 1992, and more than the 257 they won when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

  • Their current margin over Republicans — 85 seats — is the widest for either party since 1990 (charted above).

3. 🇨🇳 Jensen lover's spy ties
 
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang greets Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang after delivering a speech in Taipei, Taiwan, in 2024. Photo: Ann Wang/Reuters

The Chinese businesswoman who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang "kept in contact with an official of China's top spy agency" during their relationship, The New York Times' Jonathan Swan, Julian Barnes and Maggie Haberman report.

  • Why it matters: Alice Huang's contacts with the spy agency help explain how U.S. officials came to believe Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

🔎 Zoom in: She was in touch with an officer of China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this fall, the Times reports.

  • U.S. intelligence agencies also gathered evidence that her business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same agency.
Via Truth Social

4. 💰 Charted: AI forecast freeze
 
Data: FactSet. Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Wall Street's spending forecasts for some of the AI boom's biggest players — Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle — have leveled off, Axios' Matt Phillips writes.

  • Why it matters: Beyond the tech giants, the AI building spree has boosted profits at "picks-and-shovels" companies such as power providers and cable suppliers. Their stocks have delivered some of the buildout's most astonishing gains.

AI investment has driven S&P 500 earnings growth and overall corporate profitability to remarkably high levels.

5. 🇨🇦 Behind the scenes: Hegseth's shot at Canada
 
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks to the media last week in Caracas, Venezuela. Photo: Leonardo Fernández Viloria/Reuters

Axios White House reporter Marc Caputo writes:

The Pentagon accused Canada of failing to become a "credible partner" due to its faltering military readiness and low defense spending, according to a sharply worded fact sheet issued by the Pentagon to justify new restrictions on America's northern neighbor.

  • Why it matters: The restrictions deepen tensions between the U.S. and Canada over trade and defense, as Ottawa reconsiders billions of dollars in purchases of American weapons.

The new restraints — which don't affect defense or intelligence sharing — limit fraternization by U.S. military personnel with their Canadian counterparts at official events without prior authorization from the Pentagon, an official told Axios.

6. 💰 NEW: DNC's super PAC crackdown
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

In an announcement today, DNC Chair Ken Martin is moving to restrict candidates' ties to super PACs and dark-money groups in the party's 2028 presidential primary — a shift that could shake up the race for the White House, Axios' Holly Otterbein writes.

  • Why it matters: Most of the likely Democratic presidential candidates were expected to rely on super PACs to boost their messaging — and go after other contenders.

🔭 Zoom in: Under rules that the DNC is announcing today, Democratic presidential candidates must disavow any super PACs or dark-money groups that either back them or attack their opponents in ads.

  • If presidential hopefuls don't follow the guidelines, the DNC warns, they won't be allowed on the stage at primary debates.

A DNC official said the change is backed by progressives, including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), as well as more moderate Dems like Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.).

7. 🏛️ Snapshot: TrumpCare tease
 
Image: Truth Social

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is pitching President Trump on what El-Sayed branded "TrumpCare": a Medicare for All plan — gold insurance cards included — if he works with Democrats to pass it.

  • Nine days after El-Sayed posted the images on X (13 million views), Trump shared an image of El-Sayed's tweet on Truth Social without comment.
  • El-Sayed doubled down yesterday on NBC's "Meet the Press," saying he doesn't care what the plan is called and that if Trump wants a lasting legacy, "there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card."

🥊 Reality check: An earlier White House statement blasted El-Sayed's plan, calling it "Medicare for None."
 
 
8. 🎮 1 fun thing: $100K gamer
 
Image: Rockstar Games

An unknown video game streamer beat out 33,000+ other applicants to land a Kalshi job as a Grand Theft Auto VI researcher, Bloomberg reports.

  • The streamer — 36-year-old Cliff Savage — will make more than $100,000 to play the game to completion and report on the "real-world fallout" from the blockbuster hit.
